To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
breast cancer patients show significantly increased numbers of EPCs in their peripheral circulation and that these EPCs are recruited to the tumor by the tumor itself and not by the bone marrow.
circulating endothelial progenitors cells are increased in patients with breast cancer and are regulated by the tumor itself.
the tumor, as a source of angiogenic growth factors, is most important to recruit circulating endothelial progenitors to the site of tumor growth.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of endothelial progenitor cell in the pathogenesis of breast cancer.
the identification of a novel marker for breast cancer.
the role of circulating CD34+FLIK-1+ endothelial progenitor in breast cancer development.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
EPCs play a crucial role in breast cancer development.
EPCs are not only a prognostic factor for breast cancer, but also a new target for breast cancer therapy.
circulating EPCs may serve as a novel biomarker of breast cancer.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the release of EPCS in breast cancer patients is mainly regulated by angiogenic factors secreted by the tumor itself.
circulating CD34+FLk-1+ ECPs may work as a diagnostic tool in the diagnosis of breast cancer.
the amount of CD-34+FLK1+ cells is significantly elevated in breast cancer patients compared with healthy controls.
The main takeaway from our work is that
circulating endothelial progenitors may be used as a diagnostic biomarker of breast cancer.
the tumor is the source of angiogenic factors, and the tumor recruits endothelial progenitor cell to sites of new vessel formation.
the number of circulating EPCs is elevated in breast cancer patients with larger tumor size.
